title: Fit an exponential model from two points
aliases: exponential model from two data points
pattern: For y=A·b^x with A>0 and b>0, the ratio of two positive outputs determines the per-unit multiplier b.
applies: Two positive measurements are modeled by exponential growth or decay without an additive offset.
The inputs are distinct and use the same units.
steps: Divide y₂ by y₁ to get b^(x₂−x₁).
Solve for the positive base using b=exp(ln(y₂/y₁)/(x₂−x₁)).
Use either point to obtain A=y₁/b^x₁. If requested, report the per-unit percent change as 100(b−1)%.
pitfalls: A ratio over several input units is a multiplier for the entire interval. Convert it to one input unit before reporting growth.
An added offset y=C+A·b^x introduces a third parameter. Two points generally leave it undetermined.
checks: For x₂>x₁, increasing outputs require b>1 and decreasing outputs require 0<b<1.

example.problem: Find A and b in y=A·b^x given y=6 at x=1 and y=48 at x=4.
example.answer: The ratio gives b³=48/6=8, so b=2. From 6=A·2, A=3. Thus y=3·2^x, which gives 48 at x=4.

title: Recognize a Riemann sum as a definite integral
pattern: With xₖ=a+kΔx and Δx=(b−a)/n, the limit of Σ f(xₖ)Δx equals ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx for continuous f.
applies: A limit has an increasing number of terms, sample points filling an interval, and a factor proportional to 1/n.
The sampled function is continuous or otherwise Riemann integrable.
steps: Identify the interval from the sample points and find the width Δx.
Rewrite the summand as f(xₖ). Move the constant ratio of the prefactor to Δx outside the sum.
Replace the Riemann sum by the definite integral and evaluate if possible.
pitfalls: The prefactor 1/n equals the partition width only when the interval length is one.
The integral gives signed accumulation. Split at sign changes when the question asks for geometric area.
checks: Check that the total of n partition widths is b−a.
Check the sample points and any constant outside the integral.

example.answer: Use xₖ=3k/n and Δx=3/n on [0,3]. The prefactor is Δx/3. The limit is (1/3)∫₀³(1+x²) dx=(1/3)(3+9)=4.

title: Determine concavity and inflection points
pattern: On an interval where f″ has constant positive or negative sign, f is concave up or down, respectively. An inflection point occurs where a continuous graph changes concavity.
applies: A function is twice differentiable between a finite set of suspected transition points.
The question asks about bending or inflection, including points with a nonzero first derivative.
steps: Split the domain at points where f″ is zero or undefined.
Determine the sign of f″ on each interval.
At a candidate point, check continuity and whether concavity switches. Evaluate f to get the coordinates.
pitfalls: A zero of f″ with the same sign on both sides need not give an inflection point.
A gap in the domain provides no point on the graph.
checks: Use factored f″ or a test point in each interval.
Confirm opposite concavities on both sides of each reported inflection point.

example.problem: Find the concavity intervals and inflection points of f(x)=x⁴−6x².
example.answer: Since f″(x)=12(x−1)(x+1), the graph is concave up on (−∞,−1) and (1,∞) and down on (−1,1). The polynomial is continuous and the sign flips at both roots. The points are (−1,−5) and (1,−5).

title: Use the root test on a series
pattern: For L=limsup |aₙ|^(1/n), Σaₙ converges absolutely if L<1 and diverges if L>1. L=1 is inconclusive.
applies: The summand contains an nth power or its nth root is simpler than its successive-term ratio.
The question concerns convergence of terms that may change sign.
steps: Take the nth root of |aₙ| and simplify.
Find its limit if it exists. Use the limit superior when the roots oscillate.
Compare L with 1. If L=1, choose a different test.
pitfalls: The nth root applies to the whole absolute value, including factors outside the nth power.
A root limit of 1 occurs for both convergent and divergent series.
checks: When L<1, take L<r<1. Eventually |aₙ|≤rⁿ, so a geometric series bounds the tail.

example.answer: The nth root is (2n+5)/(5n−1), which tends to 2/5. The series converges absolutely by the root test.

title: Sum a telescoping series using finite partial sums
pattern: Differences of shifted copies of one sequence cancel inside a finite partial sum and leave boundary terms.
applies: The series has a difference form or algebra produces a difference of shifted terms.
An exact infinite sum or finite partial-sum formula is requested.
steps: Express aₙ as bₙ−bₙ₊ₖ with a fixed shift k, including any constant factor.
Write the sum through index N and align the shifted terms.
Retain the uncancelled terms at both ends. For an infinite series, then take the limit as N→∞.
pitfalls: Take the limit after finite cancellation. Separating the series into two divergent infinite sums is invalid.
A shift by k leaves k leading and k trailing terms once the partial sum is long enough.
checks: Substitute a small N into the partial-sum formula.
Check whether the trailing terms approach finite limits.

example.answer: Write each term as ½[1/(n+1)−1/(n+3)]. The N-term sum is ½[1/2+1/3−1/(N+2)−1/(N+3)]. The trailing terms vanish, giving 5/12.

title: Integrate a power series term by term
aliases: power series for an accumulation function
integrating a series and checking endpoints
pattern: Inside its radius of convergence, a power series can be integrated term by term. The radius stays the same and endpoints are checked separately.
applies: The integrand has a power series and the integration interval stays inside its radius.
A series for an antiderivative or accumulation function is requested.
steps: Expand the integrand at the intended center and state the open interval of convergence.
Integrate each monomial. Use the integration constant or lower limit to match the accumulation value.
Test the integrated series separately at each finite endpoint. Justify equality with the original function there if needed.
pitfalls: Endpoint convergence can change when integrating a series.
An integration constant matters when the lower limit differs from the expansion center.
checks: Differentiate the new series inside its interval to recover the integrand.
Check that the accumulation is zero at the lower limit.

example.problem: Find a power series for ∫₀ˣ t/(1+t²) dt and determine where the series converges.
example.answer: For |t|<1, expand t/(1+t²)=Σ[n≥0](−1)ⁿt^(2n+1). The integral is Σ[n≥0](−1)ⁿx^(2n+2)/(2n+2) for |x|<1. At x=±1 the same alternating series converges, giving the convergence interval [−1,1]. For |x|>1 the terms do not tend to zero. At |x|=1, integrating the finite geometric remainder gives an absolute error at most 1/(2N+4) after summing n=0 through N, so the endpoint sums equal the integral too.

title: Reverse the order of a double integral
aliases: change the order of a double integral
pattern: Keep the region and integrand fixed while describing the same points with the other coordinate on the outside.
applies: A double integral has variable inner bounds and the other order may simplify it.
The integrand is continuous on a bounded region, or another valid hypothesis permits changing order.
steps: Write the bounds as inequalities and sketch the region if needed.
Project onto the axis for the new outer variable.
At each fixed outer coordinate, find the new inner endpoints. Split into pieces if the bounding curves change.
Check the region in the new order and evaluate.
pitfalls: Swapping dx and dy while leaving the bounds in place usually changes the region.
A new slice can have multiple components or change its bounding curves.
checks: Check a corner and an interior point in both descriptions.
If unsure, integrate the constant 1 in both orders and compare areas.

example.problem: Reverse the order and evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫ₓ¹ e^(y²) dy dx.
example.answer: The region is 0≤x≤y≤1, so the reversed form is ∫₀¹ ∫₀ʸ e^(y²) dx dy. The inner integral is y·e^(y²). Integrating in y gives (e−1)/2.

title: Compute a vector line integral by parametrizing the path
aliases: F dot dr along a path
pattern: For an oriented curve r(t), work is ∫ F(r(t))·r′(t) dt over its parameter interval.
applies: A vector field is integrated along a piecewise smooth oriented path.
The field can be path dependent or the path can be open.
steps: Parametrize the path in the requested direction and identify the parameter limits.
Substitute r(t) into the field and compute r′(t).
Integrate their dot product. Sum the contributions for a piecewise path.
pitfalls: The speed factor ||r′(t)|| belongs to a scalar arc-length integral. Work uses the velocity vector inside the dot product.
Reversing the direction reverses the sign of the work.
checks: Verify the parameter endpoints match the stated start and finish.
Check that the dot product is a scalar function of the parameter.

example.problem: Find the work of F(x,y)=(−y,x) along r(t)=(t,t²) for t from 0 to 2.
example.answer: F(r(t))=(−t²,t) and r′(t)=(1,2t). Their dot product is t², so the work is ∫₀² t² dt=8/3.

title: Compute flux through a graph using its oriented normal
aliases: upward flux through z equals f of x y
pattern: For z=g(x,y), the upward area element is (−gₓ,−gᵧ,1) dx dy. Reverse its sign for downward orientation.
applies: The surface is a smooth graph over a known planar region.
An oriented flux integral of a continuous vector field is requested, including through an open surface.
steps: Project onto the xy-plane and identify the region.
Compute gₓ and gᵧ and choose the sign of the oriented area vector.
Evaluate the field at (x,y,g(x,y)), take its dot product with the area vector, and integrate over the projection.
pitfalls: The area vector already includes area scaling. Adding another surface-area factor double-counts it.
The divergence theorem requires a closed surface. An open graph can be integrated directly.
checks: For upward orientation, the area vector has a positive third component.
For a constant vertical field, upward flux equals its vertical component times the projected area.

example.problem: Find upward flux of F(x,y,z)=(x,2y,z) through z=2+x−y over 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤2.
example.answer: The upward area vector is (−1,1,1) dx dy. The dot product on the graph is −x+2y+2+x−y=2+y. The rectangle has width one in x, so the flux is ∫₀²(2+y) dy=6.

title: Prove uniform continuity with a Lipschitz bound
pattern: If |f(x)−f(y)|≤L|x−y| for all domain points and finite L>0, the choice δ=ε/L proves uniform continuity.
applies: The same distance bound is needed for all pairs of points in a domain.
Algebra or a bounded derivative on an interval can give a global Lipschitz constant.
steps: Bound |f(x)−f(y)| for arbitrary domain points by a constant times |x−y|.
If using the mean value theorem, ensure the segment joining the points lies in the interval and the derivative bound applies there.
For any ε>0 choose δ=ε/L and verify the implication. If L=0, the function is constant on the domain and any δ>0 works.
pitfalls: A δ that depends on x or y establishes only a local continuity statement.
A failed Lipschitz estimate alone leaves uniform continuity undecided.
checks: Check that the bound is finite across the whole domain, including any unbounded part.
Check that δ depends only on ε and the fixed bound.

example.problem: Prove f(x)=√(x+4) is uniformly continuous on [0,∞).
example.answer: For x,y≥0, rationalization gives |f(x)−f(y)|=|x−y|/(√(x+4)+√(y+4))≤|x−y|/4. For ε>0 choose δ=4ε. Then |x−y|<δ implies |f(x)−f(y)|<ε.
